title: Shopping and services
cando: compare options, choose one and ask for what you need

about.text: In this lesson you shop for your office and for yourself. You compare two models, ask for a cheaper one and ask about delivery. Then you choose between two phone plans, and explain your choice.
goals: Ask in a shop: Which is better? Is there a cheaper one? Do you deliver?
Compare two things: It's more useful. It isn't as big as the 300.
Talk about amounts: a few bottles, a little milk, fewer people, less time.
Read about a delivery service and two shops, and write which one you chose.
Choose between two phone plans, and explain your choice.

chapters.title: In a big shop
chapters.text:
In this lesson you compare things, choose one and ask for what you need.
First, you listen to Priya. She manages a small office, and the fridge in the staff kitchen is broken.
In a big shop, she looks at two fridges. She asks: Which model is better?
The assistant compares the two fridges. Then Priya asks: Is there a cheaper one?
The cheaper one is smaller, but it is good value. That means a good price for what you get.
At the end, she asks: Do you deliver? A fridge is too big to carry home.

chapters.title: Comparing, and amounts
chapters.text:
To compare two things, short words add -er: cheap, cheaper. Longer words take more: more useful, more expensive.
For one thing in a group, say the cheapest, or the most useful. This is the most useful phone in the shop.
You can also say not as big as. The 200 isn't as big as the 300. So the 300 is bigger.
For amounts, ask: can you count it? Bottles and people: a few, and fewer.
Milk, time and space: a little, and less. Say fewer people, but less milk.

chapters.title: Delivery, and two shops
chapters.text:
Next, you read a leaflet from a store. It explains its delivery service, in five steps.
Look for the words van and lorry. A lorry is much bigger than a van.
Then you read a short text that compares two shops. One is in the town centre. The other one is only online.
Read carefully for the numbers: prices, days and the maximum.
Then you write about something you bought. Say which shop you chose, and why.

chapters.title: Two phone plans
chapters.text:
In the task, your phone contract ends, and you choose between two new plans.
Ask about the difference. Then compare them: Plan B has more data, but it's more expensive.
Think about you. Do you use a little data, or a lot? How much can you pay each month?
Then choose one plan, and give two reasons. For example: It's cheaper, and the contract isn't as long.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a story or an article about shopping.
Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: You need a new fridge. Where do you buy it?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. In a shop, you can see it and ask questions. Online, it is often cheaper, and it comes to your door.

conversation.title: Which one is better?
conversation.setting: Priya manages a small office. The fridge in the staff kitchen is broken. Now she is in a big electrical shop. Two fridges are on display: the Frostway 200 and the Frostway 300.
lines: Good morning. Can I help you?
Yes, please. I need a fridge for our office. Which model is better, this one or that one?
They're very similar. They're the same brand, so the quality is the same. The main difference is the size.
What's the advantage of the big one?
The 300 has a bigger freezer, so it's more useful for a big team. It's £399.
Hmm, that's a lot. Is there a cheaper one?
This one, the 200. It isn't as big as the 300, but it's good value at £279.
Only the freezer. It's very small.
That's fine. We're a small team. We only need a little space for food and a few bottles of milk.
Then the 200 is the better choice for you.
Great, I'll take it. Do you deliver?
Yes, we deliver on weekdays, and it's free for anything over £250.
Perfect. Thank you, you've been very helpful.

questions.q: What is the main difference between the two fridges?
questions.why: The assistant says: They're the same brand, so the quality is the same. The main difference is the size.

questions.q: Why is the 200 a good choice for Priya?
questions.a: Her team is small, and it's cheaper.
questions.why: Priya's team is small, and the 200 costs £279, not £399.
The assistant says: Yes, we deliver on weekdays.

phrases.text: Which model is better, this one or that one?
phrases.use: Asking for advice about two things.

phrases.text: What's the advantage of the big one?
phrases.use: Asking what is good about one choice.
Asking for something that costs less.
Asking what is not so good.

phrases.text: It isn't as big as the 300.
phrases.use: Comparing two things: the 300 is bigger.
Asking if the shop can bring it to you.
Thanking someone who helped you a lot.

items.meaning: A light bag or box with handles. You carry your shopping in it round a shop.
items.example: I only need a few things, so I'll take a basket.

items.meaning: A group of things in a shop, put out so that people can see them.
items.example: The new phones are on display near the door.

items.meaning: One type of phone, car or machine from a company.
items.example: This model is newer, and it's quieter.

items.meaning: The name of a company's products.
items.example: Which brand of coffee do you buy?

items.meaning: How good or bad something is.
items.example: The shoes were cheap, but the quality is very good.

items.meaning: What you get for your money. Good value means a good price for what you get.
items.example: The lunch menu is good value at £6.

items.meaning: What you choose, or the things you can choose from.
items.example: There's a big choice of phones in this shop.

items.meaning: Almost the same, but not the same.
items.example: The two jackets are very similar.

items.meaning: The way two things are not the same.
items.example: What's the difference between these two printers?

items.meaning: A good thing about something. It makes it better than others.
items.example: The big advantage of this flat is the garden.

items.meaning: A bad thing about something. It makes it worse than others.
items.example: The one disadvantage is the price.

items.meaning: To take something to a person's home or workplace.
items.example: Can you deliver it on Saturday?

items.meaning: It helps you do something.
items.example: A diary is very useful at work.

items.meaning: Happy to help. A thing can be helpful too, like good advice.
items.example: The woman at the desk was very helpful.

sound.title: Short, quiet as and than
sound.explain: In a comparison, as and than are short, quiet words. Say them quickly, and don't stop on them. Put the strong sound on the important word: big, cheaper, useful. Listen, then say each group.
groups: as big as · as good as · as cheap as
cheaper than · better than · more useful than
lines: It isn't as big as the 300.
This bag is more useful than my old one.

sayIt.instructions: Say Priya's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Is every question clear?
lines: Yes, please. I need a fridge for our office. Which model is better, this one or that one?
Hmm, that's a lot. Is there a cheaper one?
That's fine. We're a small team. We only need a little space for food and a few bottles of milk.
Great, I'll take it. Do you deliver?

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Three compare the two fridges. One is about amounts.
examples: It's more useful for a big team.
It isn't as big as the 300.
We only need a little space for food and a few bottles of milk.
spot.question: Why do we say more useful, but cheaper? What does not as big as mean? Why a little space, but a few bottles?
spot.answer: Useful is a long word, so it takes more. Cheap is short, so it adds -er. Not as big as means smaller: the 300 is bigger. A little goes with space, which you cannot count. A few goes with bottles, which you can count.

rules.title: More useful, the most useful; not as … as
rule: Short words add -er: cheap, cheaper. Longer words take more: useful, more useful.
Two things: The 300 is more useful than the 200.
Three or more: the cheapest, the most useful. It's the most useful phone in the shop.
not as … as: The 200 isn't as big as the 300. (The 300 is bigger.)
After as, use the plain word: as big as, as useful as.
rules.mistake: Not: It isn't as bigger as the 300. Say: It isn't as big as the 300.

rules.title: A few, a little, fewer, less
rule: You can count it: a few bottles, a few people. Not as many: fewer.
You can't count it: a little milk, a little time. Not as much: less.
Fewer people shop here on Mondays. This fridge uses less electricity.
Ask: How many bottles? — A few. How much milk? — A little.
rules.mistake: Not: less people. Say: fewer people.

practice.q: This bag is ___ than my old one. It has more pockets.
practice.why: Useful is a long word: more useful than.

practice.q: Ana is the ___ person in our team. She always helps.
practice.why: One from a group: the most helpful.

practice.q: The small printer isn't ___ fast as the big one.
practice.why: not as … as: not as fast as.
After as, use the plain word: as big as.

practice.q: The red kettle is cheaper than the blue one. So …
options: the blue one isn't as cheap as the red one.
the red one isn't as cheap as the blue one.
the blue one is as cheap as the red one.
practice.a: the blue one isn't as cheap as the red one.
practice.why: The red one is cheaper, so the blue one is not as cheap.

practice.q: Can I have ___ milk in my tea, please?
practice.why: You can't count milk, so a little.

practice.q: There are only ___ people in the shop today.
practice.why: You can count people, so a few.

practice.q: This fridge uses ___ electricity than the old one.
practice.why: You can't count electricity, so less.

practice.q: ___ customers came in on Monday than on Saturday.
practice.why: You can count customers, so fewer.
Cheap is a short word: cheaper.

yourTurn.prompt: Compare two things you use, like two phones, two bags or two shops. Write three sentences. Use more … than, not as … as, and a few or a little.
starters: I only need a few … / a little …
yourTurn.model: My new phone is more useful than my old one, because the camera is better. My old phone wasn't as fast as this one. I only need a few apps and a little space for photos. So I chose a cheap model.

text.title: Delivery, and two shops compared
text.body:
PRACTICE LEAFLET: this store does not exist.
MILLER'S HOME STORE · HOW OUR DELIVERY SERVICE WORKS
1. Choose your things in the store or online. Payment is by card when you order.
2. Choose a day. We deliver from Monday to Saturday.
3. Small things come by van. Big things, like sofas, beds and fridges, come by lorry.
4. Tell us about access: stairs, a lift or a narrow door.
5. The driver calls you 30 minutes before.
On average, delivery takes 3 days. It is free for orders over £250.
Maximum: 2 big things in one delivery.
Nobody at home? We try again the next day. Or you can collect your order in person.

- - - - - - - -

PRACTICE: both shops are made up.
TWO SHOPS COMPARED: buying a sofa
Miller's Home Store is in the town centre. Easyseat is only online.
Easyseat is about £100 cheaper. But it has fewer models, and you can't see them in person.
Miller's has more choice: 40 sofas on display. The staff are very helpful.
Delivery from Easyseat isn't as fast. It takes about 10 days, and it costs £30.
Miller's delivers in about 3 days, and it's free.
So, for the lowest price, choose Easyseat. For more choice and faster delivery, choose Miller's.

gist.a: how the store brings things to your home
wrong: how to get a job at the store
how to pay for a sofa in cash
gist.why: The leaflet's title is: How our delivery service works.

gist.q: What does the second text compare?
gist.why: Its title is: Two shops compared: buying a sofa.

detail.q: How do big things, like fridges, come?
detail.why: The leaflet says: Big things, like sofas, beds and fridges, come by lorry.

detail.q: Nobody is at home when Miller's driver comes. What happens?
detail.a: They try again the next day.
wrong: Your order goes back to the factory.
detail.why: The leaflet says: Nobody at home? We try again the next day.

detail.a: It's cheaper, but delivery takes longer.
wrong: It has more models than Miller's.
detail.why: Easyseat is about £100 cheaper, but delivery takes about 10 days.

detail.q: Why do some people choose Miller's?
detail.a: It has more choice and faster delivery.
detail.why: The text says: For more choice and faster delivery, choose Miller's.

items.meaning: When a company brings something to your home or workplace.
items.example: Delivery is free on orders over £50.

items.meaning: Work that a company does for people, like delivery, repairs or cleaning.
items.example: The shop has a very good delivery service.

items.meaning: Money that you pay for something.
items.example: We take payment by card or in cash.

items.meaning: It is like a big car, with space at the back for things. Shops use vans to deliver.
items.example: A white van brought my new chair.

items.meaning: It is much bigger than a van. It carries heavy things by road.
items.example: The fridge came by lorry.

items.meaning: A shop, often a big one.
items.example: The new furniture store is next to the station.

items.meaning: A way to get into a place, like a door, stairs or a lift.
items.example: Access to our office is by the side door.

items.meaning: The usual or middle amount. For example, the average of 2, 3 and 4 is 3.
items.example: On average, delivery takes three days.

items.meaning: The biggest number or amount that is allowed or possible.
items.example: The maximum is two big things in one delivery.

items.meaning: You go there yourself, not by phone, email or post.
items.example: You can pay online or in person at the store.

model.title: Which shop I chose, and why
model.body:
I needed a new sofa for my flat, so I compared two shops.
Easyseat was about £100 cheaper, but I chose Miller's Home Store.
First, I wanted to sit on the sofas in person. Online, you only see photos.
Miller's had more choice, and the staff were very helpful.
Delivery was faster, too. My sofa came by lorry three days later.
It wasn't the cheaper one, but it was the better choice for me.

write.task: Think of something you bought, like a phone, a bag or a course. Compare two shops or two choices. Say which one you chose, and why. It can be real or made up.
write.starter: I needed a new …, so I compared …
checklist: I compared two shops or two choices: cheaper, more useful, not as … as.
I said which one I chose.
I gave two reasons, with because or so.
I wrote about the price, the choice or the delivery.

card.title: Two phone plans
card.situation: Your phone contract ends this month. The phone shop offers you two plans. Plan A is £10 a month, with 5 GB of data, for 12 months. Plan B is £16 a month, with 30 GB of data, for 24 months.
card.goal: Ask the assistant about the two plans. Compare them, choose one, and explain your choice with two reasons.

phrases: What's the difference between Plan A and Plan B?
Plan B has more data, but it's more expensive.
Plan A isn't as long as Plan B. It's only 12 months.
I only use a little data, so Plan A is better for me.
prepare.notes: Make notes first. How much data do you use: a little, or a lot? How much can you pay each month? Then choose a plan, and write two reasons.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is the assistant in the phone shop. Ask about the two plans, compare them and choose one. Then tell the class which plan you chose, and why.
doIt.wehel: You are an assistant in a phone shop. I need a new phone plan. There are two plans. Plan A is £10 a month, with 5 GB of data, for 12 months. Plan B is £16 a month, with 30 GB of data, for 24 months. Answer my questions. Then ask me which plan I choose, and why. Use simple English.

model.title: Choosing a plan
lines: Yes, please. My contract ends this month. What's the difference between these two plans?
Plan B has more data: 30 GB. Plan A only has 5 GB.
Yes, it's £16 a month. Plan A is £10.
And how long is each contract?
Plan A is 12 months, and Plan B is 24 months.
I only use a little data, for email and maps. I don't watch films on my phone.
Then Plan A is probably the better choice for you.
I think so too. It's cheaper, and the contract isn't as long. I'll take Plan A, please.
Good choice. Can I have your name, please?
compare: Did you ask about the difference between the two plans?
Did you compare them: cheaper, more expensive, not as long as?
Did you say how much you use: a little data, a few calls?
Did you choose one and give two reasons?

canDo: I can ask in a shop: Which is better? Is there a cheaper one? Do you deliver?
I can compare two things with more … than and not as … as.
I can talk about amounts with a few, a little, fewer and less.
I can read about a delivery service and a comparison of two shops.
I can choose between two options and explain my choice.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first picture. What are the people buying? Where do you think they shop?
reading.talk: Did the people in the story make a good choice? Where do you like to shop, and why? Write two or three sentences, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.q: The train is ___ than the bus, but it's faster.
quiz.why: Expensive is a long word: more expensive than.
not as … as: not as big as.

quiz.q: Can I have ___ sugar in my coffee, please?
quiz.why: You can't count sugar, so a little.

quiz.q: ___ people shop here on Mondays than on Saturdays.
quiz.why: You can count people, so fewer.

quiz.q: The two phones are very ___ . They look almost the same.
This one is too expensive. Is there a ___ one?
quiz.why: Cheap is a short word: cheaper.

quiz.q: Do you ___ ? I can't carry a sofa home on the bus!
quiz.why: Deliver: bring it to your home.

quiz.q: I'm leaving early ___ I can get a good seat.
quiz.why: So that + a sentence says why: so that I can get a seat.

quiz.q: I've decided. I'm ___ to book a holiday in May.
quiz.why: A decision: I'm going to + a verb.

quiz.q: We ___ two hours in a traffic jam yesterday.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the shop conversation in pairs. Then change the thing: two phones, two chairs, two kettles. Each learner asks: Which is better? Is there a cheaper one? Do you deliver?
Day 2: show two similar things, such as two pens, two phones or two bags. Learners compare them with more … than and not as … as. Then a quick game: you say a word, and they answer a few or a little.
Day 3: the task. You are the assistant in the phone shop. Each learner asks about the two plans, chooses one and explains why.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and read two learners' texts about which shop they chose aloud.
